Let us take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish, we can produce infinitely many large positive integers. Let us observe a few : 2  3  11 = 66 7  11 = 77 7  11  23 = 1771 3  7  111  23 = 5313 2  3  7  111  23 = 10626 23  3  73 = 8232 A 22  3  7  111  23 = 21252 N Now, let us suppose collection of all prime numbers. When we take two or more primes A from this collection and multiply them, do we get prime number again? or do we get composite number? So, if we multiply all these primes in all possible waysG, we will get an infinite collection of composite numbers. Now, let us consider the converse of this statement i.e. if we take a N composite number can it be written as a product of prime numbers? The following theorem answers the question. A Theorem-1.2 : (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) : Every composite number can be L expressed (factorised) as a product of primes and this factorization is unique, apart E from the order in which the prime factors occur. T This gives us the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic which says that every composite number can be factorized as a p roduct of primes. To say it more clearly, any given composite , number can be factorized as a product of prime numbers in a ‘unique’ way, except for the order T in which the primes occur. For example, when we factorize 210, we regard 2 3  5  7 as R same as 3  5  7  2, or any other possible order in which these primes are written. That is, given any composite number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as E long as we are not particular about the order in which the primes occur. C In general, given a composite number x, we factorize it as x = p .p .p .....p , where 1 2 3 n pS, p , p ...., p are primes and written in ascending order, i.e., p  p ... p . If we express 1 2 3 n 1 2 n all these equal primes in simplified form, we will get powers of primes. Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number is factorised, is unique. For example, 27300 = 2  2  3  5  5  7 13 = 22  3  52  7  13 Do This Express 2310 as a product of prime factors. Also see how your friends have factorized the number. Let us apply Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic Example 3. Consider the numbers of the form 4n where n is a natural number. Check whether there is any value of n for which 4n ends with zero? Solution : If 4n is to end with zero for a natural number n, it should be divisible by 2 and 5. This means that the prime factorisation of 4n should contain the prime number 5 and 2. But it is not A possible because 4n = (2)2n. So 2 is the only prime in the factorisation of 4n. Since 5 is not present N in the prime factorization, there is no natural number 'n' for which '4n' ends with the digit zero. Dasarathi was a telugu poet and also a freedom fighter. N Albert Einstein was a physicist who proposed theory of relativity. Maryam Mirzakhan is the only womanA mathematican to win Fields medal. We classify the individuals first as a member of larger recognizable group then with L specific character and interest. People classify and categorize the world around them, in order to make sense of their environment and theEir relationships to others. Books in the library are arranged according to the subject, so that we can find them T quickly. In chemistry the elements are categorized in groups and classes to study their general , properties T Your mathematics syllabus for tenth class has been divided into 14 chapters under R different headings. E Dental Formula C Observe the set of human teeth. It is S classified into 4-types according to their functions. (i) Incisors (ii) Canines (iii) Premolars and (iv) Molars The teeth set is classified into Incisors, Canines, Premolars and Molars on the basis of chewing method. Therefore, sets are generally denoted by N capital letters of English alphabet A, B, C..... A For example, M is the set of molars of our teeth. L We can write this set as M={first molar, second molar, third molar}. E Let us look at another example. Q is the set of quadrilaterals with at least two equal T sides. Then, we can write this set as Q ={square, rectangle,, rhombus, parallelogram, kite, isosceles trapezium} T Here, we are writing a set by listing the elements in it. In such case, the set is said to be R written in the “roster form”. E In the above two examples, let us discuss belongingness of the elements and its repre- sentatioCn. Suppose, if we want to say “second molar is in the set of molars”, then we can repre- sent this as “second molar  M”. Does “square” belong to the set M in the above examples? Then, how do we denote this? When we say “ square is not in the set M”, we denote as “square  M”. pages.text: Chapter Pair of Linear Equations 4 in Two Variables A N 4.1 Introduction A One day, Siri went to a book shop with her father and bought 3 notebooks and 2 pens. Her G father paid `80 for them. Her friend Laxmi liked the notebooks and pens. So, she too bought 4 notebooks and 3 pens of the same kind for `110. Now her classmates Rubina liked the pens whereas N Joseph liked the notebooks. They asked Siri the cost of the pen and the notebook separately. But, Siri did not know the costs separately. How will they find the costs of these items? A In this example, the cost of a notebook and a pen are not known. These are unknown L quantities. We come across many such situations in our day-to-day life. E Think & Discuss T Two situations are given below: , (i) The cost of 1kg potatoes and 2kg tomatoes was `30 on a certain day. After two days, T the cost of 2kg potatoes and 4kg tomatoes was found to be `66. R (ii) The coach of a cricket team of M.K.Nagar High School buys 3 bats and 6 balls for `3900. Later he buys one more bat and 2 balls for `1300. E Identify the unknowns in each situation. We observe that there are two unknowns in each case. C 4.1.1 How Do We Find Unknown Quantities? chapters.fullText: Chapter Pair of Linear Equations 4 in Two Variables A N 4.1 Introduction A One day, Siri went to a book shop with her father and bought 3 notebooks and 2 pens. Her G father paid `80 for them. Her friend Laxmi liked the notebooks and pens. So, she too bought 4 notebooks and 3 pens of the same kind for `110. Now her classmates Rubina liked the pens whereas N Joseph liked the notebooks. They asked Siri the cost of the pen and the notebook separately. But, Siri did not know the costs separately. How will they find the costs of these items? A In this example, the cost of a notebook and a pen are not known. These are unknown L quantities. We come across many such situations in our day-to-day life. E Think & Discuss T Two situations are given below: , (i) The cost of 1kg potatoes and 2kg tomatoes was `30 on a certain day. After two days, T the cost of 2kg potatoes and 4kg tomatoes was found to be `66. R (ii) The coach of a cricket team of M.K.Nagar High School buys 3 bats and 6 balls for `3900. Later he buys one more bat and 2 balls for `1300. E Identify the unknowns in each situation. We observe that there are two unknowns in each case. C 4.1.1 How Do We Find Unknown Quantities? SIn the introduction, Siri bought 3 notebooks and 2 pens for `80. How can we find the cost of a notebook or the cost of a pen? Rubina and Joseph tried to guess. Rubina said that price of each notebook could be `25. Then three notebooks would cost `75 and the two pens would cost `5. In that case each pen could be for `2.50. Joseph felt that `2.50 for one pen was too less. In his opinion, it should be at least `16. Then the price of each notebook would also be `16. We can see that there can be many possible values for the price of a notebook and of a pen so that the total cost is `80. So, how do we find the price at which Siri and Laxmi bought them? By using only Siri's situation, we cannot find the costs. We have to use Laxmi's situation also. 77 Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables 4.1.2 Using Both Equations Together Laxmi also bought the same types of notebooks and pens as Siri. She paid 110 for 4 notebooks and 3 pens. So, we have two situations which can be represented as follows: A (i) Cost of 3 notebooks + Cost of 2 pens = 80. (ii) Cost of 4 notebooks + Cost of 3 pens = 110. N Does this help us find the cost of a pen and a notebook? A Consider the prices mentioned by Rubina. If the price of one notebook is 25 and the G price of one pen is 2.50 then, The cost of 4 notebooks would be : 4 × 25 N= 100 And the cost for 3 pens would be : 3 × 2.50 = 7.50 A If Rubina is right then Laxmi should have paid 100 + 7.50 = 107.50 but she paid 110. L Now, consider the prices mentionEed by Joseph. The cost of 4 notebooks, if one is for 16, would be : 4 × 16 = 64 T And the cost for 3 pens, if one is for 16, would be : 3 × 16 = 48 , If Joseph is right thTen Laxmi should have paid 64 + 48 = 112 but this is more than the price she paid. R So what do we do? How to find the exact cost of the notebook and the pen? E If we have only one equation but two unknowns (variables), we can find many solutions. C So, when we have two variables, we need at least two independent equations to get a unique Ssolution. One way to find the values of unknown quantities is by using the Model method. In this method, rectangles or portions of rectangles are often used to represent the unknowns. Let us look at the first situation using the model method: Step-1 : Represent a notebook by and a pen by . Later he buys one more bat and 2 balls for `1300. E Identify the unknowns in each situation. We observe that there are two unknowns in each case. C 4.1.1 How Do We Find Unknown Quantities? SIn the introduction, Siri bought 3 notebooks and 2 pens for `80. How can we find the cost of a notebook or the cost of a pen? Rubina and Joseph tried to guess. Rubina said that price of each notebook could be `25. Then three notebooks would cost `75 and the two pens would cost `5. In that case each pen could be for `2.50. Joseph felt that `2.50 for one pen was too less. In his opinion, it should be at least `16. Then the price of each notebook would also be `16. We can see that there can be many possible values for the price of a notebook and of a pen so that the total cost is `80. So, how do we find the price at which Siri and Laxmi bought them? By using only Siri's situation, we cannot find the costs. We have to use Laxmi's situation also. 77 Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables 4.1.2 Using Both Equations Together Laxmi also bought the same types of notebooks and pens as Siri. She paid 110 for 4 notebooks and 3 pens. So, we have two situations which can be represented as follows: A (i) Cost of 3 notebooks + Cost of 2 pens = 80. (ii) Cost of 4 notebooks + Cost of 3 pens = 110. N Does this help us find the cost of a pen and a notebook? A Consider the prices mentioned by Rubina. If the price of one notebook is 25 and the G price of one pen is 2.50 then, The cost of 4 notebooks would be : 4 × 25 N= 100 And the cost for 3 pens would be : 3 × 2.50 = 7.50 A If Rubina is right then Laxmi should have paid 100 + 7.50 = 107.50 but she paid 110. They want to leave space of equal width all around the court for the spectators. What would be the width of the space for spectators? Would it be enough? Since, the LHS of the above equations (1) and (2) are quadratic polynomials and the RHS is 0 they are called quadratic equations. In this chapter we will study quadratic equations and methods to find their roots. 5.2 Quadratic Equations 2 A quadratic equation in the variable x is an equation of the form ax + bx + c = 0, where a, 2 b, c are real numbers and a  0. For example, 2x + x  300 = 0 is a quadratic equation, 2 2 2 Similarly, 2x  3x + 1 = 0, 4x  3x + 2 = 0 and 1  x + 300 = 0 are also quadratic equations. In fact, any equation of the form p(x)  0, where p(x) is a polynomial of degree 2, is a quadratic equation. When we write the terms of p(x) in descending order of their degrees, then 2 we get the standard form of the equation. That is, ax + bx + c = 0, a  0 is called the standard 2 form of a quadratic equation and y = p(x) = ax + bx + c is called a quadratic function. Now, we need to find the value of x. S 2 Consider the quadratic equation 2x – 3x + 1 = 0. If we replace x by 1. Then, we get 2 2 × (1) – (3 × 1) + 1 = 0 = RHS of the equation. Since x = 1 satisfies the equation , we say that 2 1 is a root / solution of the quadratic equation 2x – 3x + 1 = 0. 2 In general, a real number  is called a root of the quadratic equation ax + bx + c = 0, 2 if a + b + c = 0. They are (1, 6), (–1, –6); N (2, 3); (–2, –3). From the list, it is clear that the pair (–2, –3) will satisfy our condition A p + q = –5 and p × q = 6. pages.text: Chapter 6 Progressions A N 6.1 Introduction A You might have observed that in nature, many things follow a certain pattern such as the petals of a sunflower, the cells of a honeycomb, the grains oGn a maize cob, the spirals on a pineapple and on a pine cone etc. N Can you see a pattern in each of the above given example? We can see the natural A patterns have a repetition which is not progressive. The identical petals of the sunflower are equidistantly grown. In a honeycomb identical hexagonal shaped cells are arranged symmetrically L around each hexagonal cell. Similarly, you can find out other natural patterns in spirals of E pineapple.... T You can look for some other patterns in nature. Some examples are: (i) List of the last digits (d,igits in unit place) taken from the values of 4, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46 ..... is T 4, 6, 4, 6, 4, 6, ...... R (ii) Mary is doing problems on patterns as a part of preparing for a bank exam. One of them is “finEd the next two terms in the following pattern”. C1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 20, 22 ....... (iii) Usha applied for a job and got selected. She has been offered a job with a starting S monthly salary of ` 8000, with an annual increment of `500. Her salary (in rupees) for 1st, 2nd, 3rd ... years will be 8000, 8500, 9000 ..... respectively. (iv) The lengths of the rungs of a ladder decrease uniformly by 2 cm from bottom to top. The bottom rung is 45 cm in length. The lengths (in cm) of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, .... 8th rung from the bottom to the top are 45, 43, 41, 39, 37, 35, 33, 31 respectively. Can you see any relationship between the terms in the pattern of numbers written above? Pattern given in example (i) has a repetitive pattern where 4 and 6 are repeating alternatively. (e) A pair of rabbits are too young to produce in their first month. In the second, and every subsequent month, they produce a new pair. Each new pair of rabbits produce a new pair in their second month and in every subsequent month (see the figure below). Assuming no rabbit dies, the number of pairs of rabbits at the start of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ....., 6th month, respectively are : 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 A N 1 A 1 G 2 N A 3 L 5 E T 8 , In the examples above, we observe some patterns. In some of them, we find that the T succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number and in others by multiplying with a R fixed number. In another, we find that they are squares of consecutive numbers and so on. In thiEs chapter, we shall discuss some of these patterns in which succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term or multiplying the preceding term by a C fixed number. These patterns are called as arithmetic and geometric progressions respectively. We shall also see how to find their nth term and the sum of n consecutive terms for a general value S of ‘n’ and use this knowledge in solving some daily life problems. History : Evidence is found that by 400 BCE, Babylonians knew of Arithmetic and geometric progressions. According to Boethins (570 CE), these progressions were known to early Greek writers. Among the Indian mathematicians, Aryabhatta (470 CE) was the first to give formula for the sum of squares and cubes of natural numbers in his famous work Aryabhatiyam written around 499 CE. He also gave the formula for finding the sum of n terms of an Arithmetic th Progression starting with p term. Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (598 CE), Mahavira (850 CE) and Bhaskara (1114-1185 CE) also considered the sums of squares and cubes. chapters.fullText: Chapter 6 Progressions A N 6.1 Introduction A You might have observed that in nature, many things follow a certain pattern such as the petals of a sunflower, the cells of a honeycomb, the grains oGn a maize cob, the spirals on a pineapple and on a pine cone etc. N Can you see a pattern in each of the above given example? We can see the natural A patterns have a repetition which is not progressive. The identical petals of the sunflower are equidistantly grown. In a honeycomb identical hexagonal shaped cells are arranged symmetrically L around each hexagonal cell. Similarly, you can find out other natural patterns in spirals of E pineapple.... lessonSections.fullText: Chapter 6 Progressions A N 6.1 Introduction A You might have observed that in nature, many things follow a certain pattern such as the petals of a sunflower, the cells of a honeycomb, the grains oGn a maize cob, the spirals on a pineapple and on a pine cone etc. N Can you see a pattern in each of the above given example? We can see the natural A patterns have a repetition which is not progressive. The identical petals of the sunflower are equidistantly grown. In a honeycomb identical hexagonal shaped cells are arranged symmetrically L around each hexagonal cell. Similarly, you can find out other natural patterns in spirals of E pineapple.... T You can look for some other patterns in nature. Some examples are: (i) List of the last digits (d,igits in unit place) taken from the values of 4, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46 ..... is T 4, 6, 4, 6, 4, 6, ...... Her salary (in rupees) for 1st, 2nd, 3rd ... years will be 8000, 8500, 9000 ..... respectively. (iv) The lengths of the rungs of a ladder decrease uniformly by 2 cm from bottom to top. The bottom rung is 45 cm in length. The lengths (in cm) of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, .... 8th rung from the bottom to the top are 45, 43, 41, 39, 37, 35, 33, 31 respectively. In the second, and every subsequent month, they produce a new pair. Each new pair of rabbits produce a new pair in their second month and in every subsequent month (see the figure below). Assuming no rabbit dies, the number of pairs of rabbits at the start of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ....., 6th month, respectively are : 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 A N 1 A 1 G 2 N A 3 L 5 E T 8 , In the examples above, we observe some patterns. In some of them, we find that the T succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number and in others by multiplying with a R fixed number. In another, we find that they are squares of consecutive numbers and so on. In thiEs chapter, we shall discuss some of these patterns in which succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term or multiplying the preceding term by a C fixed number. These patterns are called as arithmetic and geometric progressions respectively. We shall also see how to find their nth term and the sum of n consecutive terms for a general value S of ‘n’ and use this knowledge in solving some daily life problems. History : Evidence is found that by 400 BCE, Babylonians knew of Arithmetic and geometric progressions. According to Boethins (570 CE), these progressions were known to early Greek writers. Among the Indian mathematicians, Aryabhatta (470 CE) was the first to give formula for the sum of squares and cubes of natural numbers in his famous work Aryabhatiyam written around 499 CE. He also gave the formula for finding the sum of n terms of an Arithmetic th Progression starting with p term. Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (598 CE), Mahavira (850 CE) and Bhaskara (1114-1185 CE) also considered the sums of squares and cubes. keyPoints: In the second, and every subsequent month, they produce a new pair.
Each new pair of rabbits produce a new pair in their second month and in every subsequent month (see the figure below).
In some of them, we find that the T succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number and in others by multiplying with a R fixed number.
In another, we find that they are squares of consecutive numbers and so on.
In thiEs chapter, we shall discuss some of these patterns in which succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term or multiplying the preceding term by a C fixed number.
These patterns are called as arithmetic and geometric progressions respectively.
We shall also see how to find their nth term and the sum of n consecutive terms for a general value S of ‘n’ and use this knowledge in solving some daily life problems.
History : Evidence is found that by 400 BCE, Babylonians knew of Arithmetic and geometric progressions.
According to Boethins (570 CE), these progressions were known to early Greek writers.
Among the Indian mathematicians, Aryabhatta (470 CE) was the first to give formula for the sum of squares and cubes of natural numbers in his famous work Aryabhatiyam written around 499 CE.

summary: th 6.6 n term of a G.P. Let us examine a problem. The number of bacteria in a certain petri dish culture triples every hour. If there were 30 bacteria present in the petri dish originally, then what would be the number of bacteria in fourth hour? To answer this, let us first see what the number of bacteria in second hour would be.

A Since for every hour it triples N No.of bacteria in Second hour = 3 × no.of bacteria in first hour 1 A = 3 × 30 = 30 × 3 (2-1) = 30 × 3 G = 90 N No.of bacteria in third hour = 3 × no.of bacteria in second hour A = 3 × 90 = 30 × (3×3) 2 (3-1) = 30 × 3 L= 30 × 3 = 270 E No.of bacteria in fourth hour = 3 × no.of bacteria in third hour T = 3 × 270 = 30 × (3×3×3) 3 (4-1) ,= 30 × 3 = 30 × 3 T = 810 R Observe that we are getting a list of numbers E30, 90, 270, 810, ....

A G She wants to find out the height of that tree but she is not sure N how to find it. Meanwhile, her uncle arrives at home. Snigdha A requests her uncle to help her to B C E L find the height of the tree. He E thinks for a while and then asks her to bring a mirror. He places it on the ground at a certain distance from the base of the tree. He then asked Snigdha to stand on the otherside of the mirror T at such a position from where she is able to see the top of the tree in that mirror. When we draw the figu,re from (AB) girl to the mirror (C) and mirror to the tree (DE) as T above, we observe triangles ABC and DEC. Now, what can you say about these two triangles? Are they congruent? No, because although they have the same shape their sizes are R different. Do you know what we call the geometrical figures which have the same shape, but are not necessarEily of the same size? They are called similar figures. How do we know the height of a tree or a mountain? How do we know the distances of C far away objects such as Sun or Moon? Do you think these can be measured directly with the Shelp of a measuring tape? The fact is that all these heights and distances have been found out using the idea of indirect measurements which is based on the principle of similarity of figures. 8.2 Similar Figures (i) (ii) (iii) Observe the object (car) in the figure (i). We find that the figure is distorted. Can you say that they are similar? No, they have same shape, yet they are not similar. Think what a photographer does when she prints photographs of different sizes from the same film (negative) ? You might have heard about stamp size, passport size andA post card size photographs. She generally takes a photograph on a small size film, say 35 mm., and then N enlarges it into a bigger size, say 45 mm (or 55 mm). We observe that every line segment of the smaller photograph is enlarged in the ratio of 35 : 45 (or 35 : 55). FurthAer, in the two photographs of different sizes, we can see that the corresponding angles are equal. So, the photographs are G similar. T The ratio of the corresponding sides is referred to as scale or scale factor (or) representative R factor). In real life, blue prints for the construction of a building are prepared using a suitable scale factor. E Think and Discuss C Give some more examples from your daily life where scale factor is used. Circles with same radius are congruent and those with different radii are not congruent. But, as all circles have same shape and different size, they are all similar. pages.text: Chapter 9 Tangents and Secants to a Circle A 9.1 Introduction N We have seen that two lines in a plane may intersect at a point or may not intersect. In A some situations, they may coincide with each other. G O N Similarly, what are the possible relative positAions of a curve and a line given in a plane? A curve may be a parabola as you have seen in polynomials or a simple closed curve like a “circle” L which is a collection of all those points on a plane that are at a constant distance from a fixed point. E Y T X , T You might hRave seen circular objects rolling on a plane creating a path. For example; bicycle wheel on a sandy field, wheels of train on the track etc., where a circle as well as a line are involved.E LCet us observe the relative positions of a circle and a line are given in a plane. 9S.1.1 A Line and A Circle You are asked to draw a circle and a line on a paper. Abhiram argues that there can only be 3 possible ways of presenting them on a paper. Consider a circle with centre ‘O’ and a line PQ. The three possibilities are given in the following figures. P P P A A O O O B (i) Q (ii) Q (iii) Q 229 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222333777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333185 PPPMMM

In Fig.(i), the line PQ and the circle have no common point. In this case, PQ is a non- intersecting line with respect to the circle. In Fig.(ii), the line PQ intersects the circle at two points A and B. It forms a chord AB with its end points A and B on the circle. In this case, the line PQ is a secant of the circle. In Fig.(iii), there is only one point A, common to the line PQ and the circle. This line is called a tangent to the circle. A You can see that there cannot be any other position of the line with respect to the circle. N We will study the existence of tangents to a circle and also study their properties and constructions. Do you know? A The word ‘tangent’ comes from the latin word ‘tangereG’, which means to touch and was introduced by Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583. N Do This A q l i. Draw a circle with any radius. Draw four tangents at different p L m points. How many more tangents can you draw to this circle? E ii. How many tangents can you draw to a circle from a point away O from it? T iii. In the adjacent figure, whi ch lines are tangents to the circle? , T 9.2 Tangents of a Circle R We can see that tangent to a circle can be drawn at any point on the circle. How many tangents can be drawn at any point on the circle? E To understand this let us consider the following activity. C Activity S Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of A the circular wire, so that the system can rotate about the point P in a plane. The circular wire represents a circle A11 A1 A P and the straight wire AB represents a line B O Q intersects the circle at point P. 1 Place the system on a table and gently Q 2 rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of P O the straight wire as shown in the figure. The wire intersects the Q B 3 circular wire at P and at one of the points Q , Q or Q etc. So 1 2 3 while it generally intersects circular wire at two points one of B11 B1 which is P in one particular position, it intersects the circle only at 230 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222333888 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333185 PPPMMM

the point P (See position AB of AB). This is the position of a tangent at the point P to the circle. You can check that in all other positions of AB, it will intersect the circle at P at another point. ThusABis a tangent to the circle at P.. We see that there is only one tangent to the circle at point P. Moving wire AB in either direction from this position makes it cut the circular wire in two A points. All these are therefore secants. Tangent is a special case of a secant where the two points of intersection of a line with a circle coincide. N Do This A Draw a circle and a secant PQ to the circle on a paper as shGown P in the figure. Draw various lines parallel to the secant on both sides of it. N What happens to the length of chord coming closer and closer to the centre of the circle? A A O What is the longest chord? L How many tangents can you draw to a circle, which are parallel to each other ? E Q The common point of a tangeTnt and the circle is called the point of contact and the tangent is said to touch the circle at the common point. Observe the tangents to ,the circle in the figures given below: T R E C SHow many tangents can you draw to a circle at a point on it? How many tangents can you draw to the circle in all? See the point of contact. Draw radii from the points of contact. Do you see anything special about the angle between the tangents and the radii at the points of contact. All appear to be perpendicular to the corresponding tangents. We can also prove it. Let us see how. Theorem-9.1 : The tangent at any point of a circle is A perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Given : A circle with centre ‘O’ and a tangent XY to the O circle at a point P and OP radius. To prove : OP is perpendicular to XY. i.e XY is tangent to circle P Y 231 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222333999 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333185 PPPMMM

 A Proof : Take a point Q on XY other than P and join O and Q. The point Q must lie outside the circle (why?) (Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY becomes a secant and not a tangent to O the circle) Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius OP of the circle [Why?] A P Q Y i.e., OQ > OP. N This must happen for all points on the line XY. It is therefore true that OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the XY. A As a perpendicular is the shortest in length among all line segments drawn from a point to the line (Activity 5.3 of 7th class). G Therefore OP is perpendicular to XY. N i.e., OP  XY Hence, proved. A Note : The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also called the ‘normal to L the circle at the point’. E Try This T How can you prove th e converse of the above theorem. , “If a line in the planTe of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at its endpoint on the circle, then the line is tangent to the circle”. R We can find some more results using the above theorem E (i) Since there can be only one perpendicular OP at the point P, it follows that one and only C one tangent can be drawn to a circle at a given point on the circle. S(ii) Since there can be only one perpendicular to XY at the point P, it follows that the perpendicular to a tangent to a circle at its point of contact passes through the centre. Think about these. Discuss these among your friends and with your teachers. 9.2.1 Construction of Tangent to a Circle How can we construct a line that would be tangent to a circle at a given point on it? We use what we just found i.e. the tangent has to be perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. To draw a tangent through the point of contact we need to draw a line prependicular to the radius at that point. To draw this radius we need to know the center of the circle. Let us see the steps for this construction. 232 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222444000 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333185 PPPMMM

Solution : Tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (Theorem 9.1) Here, PA is tangent segment and OA is radius of circle  OA  PA OAP  90 Now, in OAP, OP 2 = OA 2 + PA 2 (pythagoras theorem) A P 10 2 = 6 2 + PA 2 10 6 2 100 = 36 + PA O 2 PA = 100 - 36 = 64 PA = 64 = 8 cm. 233 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222444111 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333185 PPPMMM

T 9.3 Number of tangents to a circle from any point To get an idea of the n,umber of tangents from a point in a plane, let us perform the T following activity. R Activity E (i) Draw a circle on a paper. Take a point P CP inside it. Can you draw a tangent to the circle through this point ? You will O Sfind that all the lines through this point intersect the circle in two points. What are these ? These are all secants of a (i) circle. So, it is not possible to draw any tangent to a circle through a point P inside it. (See the adjacent figure) (ii) Next, take a point P on the circle and draw tangents through this point. You O have observed that there is only one tangent to the circle at a such a point. (See the adjacent figure) (ii) 234 Tangents and Secants to a Circle XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222444222 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::333186 PPPMMM

(iii) Now, take a point P outside the circle A and try to draw tangents to the circle from this point. What do you observe? You will find that you can draw exactly O P two tangents to the circle through this A B point (See the adjacent figure) (iii) Now, we can summarise these facts as follows : N Case (i): There is no tangent to a circle passing through a point inside the circle. A Case(ii): There is one and only one tangent to a circle at a point on the circle. Case(iii): There are exactly two tangents to a circle througGh a point outside the circle. In this case, A and B are the points of contacts of the tangents PA and PB N respectively. The length of the segment from the external point P and the point of contact with the A circle is called the length of the tangent from the point P to the circle. L Note that in the above figure (iii), PA and PB are the length of the tangents from P to the circle. What is the relation between lEengths PA and PB? chapters.fullText: Chapter 9 Tangents and Secants to a Circle A 9.1 Introduction N We have seen that two lines in a plane may intersect at a point or may not intersect. In A some situations, they may coincide with each other. G O N Similarly, what are the possible relative positAions of a curve and a line given in a plane? A curve may be a parabola as you have seen in polynomials or a simple closed curve like a “circle” L which is a collection of all those points on a plane that are at a constant distance from a fixed point. E Y T X , T You might hRave seen circular objects rolling on a plane creating a path. For example; bicycle wheel on a sandy field, wheels of train on the track etc., where a circle as well as a line are involved.E LCet us observe the relative positions of a circle and a line are given in a plane. 9S.1.1 A Line and A Circle You are asked to draw a circle and a line on a paper. Abhiram argues that there can only be 3 possible ways of presenting them on a paper. Consider a circle with centre ‘O’ and a line PQ. The three possibilities are given in the following figures. It forms a chord AB with its end points A and B on the circle. In this case, the line PQ is a secant of the circle. In Fig.(iii), there is only one point A, common to the line PQ and the circle. We use them in real life situations to identify what we need and what is to be measured G or estimated. For example, to find the quantity of paint required to white wash a room, we need the N surface area and not the volume. To find the number of bags that are required to store grain, we need the volume and not the area. A Try This L E 1. Consider the following situations. We can observe in our real life also like wooden things, house items, medicine capsules, bottles, oil-tankers etc. We eat ice-cream in our daily A life. Can you tell how many solid figures are there in it? It is usually made up of cone and hemisphere. G Lets take another example, an oil-tanker / N water-tanker. Is it a single shaped object? You may guess that it is made up of a cylinder with two A hemispheres at it ends. If you want to find the surface areasL or volumes or capacities of such objects, how would E you do it? We cannot classify these shapes under any of the solids you have already studied. T As we have seen, the oil-tanker was made up of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck at either end. It will look like the fol lowing figure: , T R E If we consider the surface of the newly formed C object, we would be able to see only the curved surfaces of the two hemispheres and the curved surface S of the cylinder. TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder + CSA of other hemisphere Here ,TSA and CSA stand for ‘total surface area’ and ‘curved surface area’ respectively. 10.3 Volume of Combination of Solids Let us understand volume of a combined solid through an example. Suresh runs an industry in a shed which is in the shape of a cuboid surmounted by a half cylinder. The base A of the shed is of dimensions 7 m. 15 m. and the height of N the cuboidal portion is 8 m. Find the volume of air that the A shed can hold? Further, suppose the machinery in the 3 shed occupies a total space of 300 m and there are 20 G 3 workers, each of whom occupies about 0.08 m space on an average. Then how much air is in the shed ? N The volume of air inside the shed (when thAere are neither people nor machinery) is given by the volume of air inside the cuboid and inside the half L cylinder taken together. The length, breadth and height of the cuboid are 15 m., 7 m. and 8 m. E respectively. Also the diameter of the half cylinder is 7 m. and its height is 15 m. T 1 So, the required volume= volume of the cuboid + volume of the cylinder.. 2 ,  1 22 7 7  T 1578    15 m3    2 7 2 2  R 3 = 1128.75m . E 3 Next, the toal space occupied by the machinery = 300 m . ACnd the total space occupied by the workers = 200.08 m 3 3 = 1.6m S Therefore, the volume of the air, inside the shed when there are machinery and workers = 1128.75 (300.00 + 1.60) 3 = 1128.75 - 301.60 = 827.15 m Note : In calculating the surface area of combination of solids, we can not add the surface areas of the two solids because some part of the surface areas disappears or coincides in the process of joining them. However, this will not be the case when we calculate the volume. E T , T R 10.4 Conversion of Solid from One Shape to Another E A women self help group (DWACRA) prepares candles by melting C down cuboid shape wax. In medicine factory, medicines in different S shapes (spherical, capsules etc) are made by using bulk drug raw material which is in the shape of a cuboid / sphere. In gun factories, spherical bullets are made by melting solid cube of lead, goldsmith prepares various ornaments by melting cubiod gold biscuts. In all these cases, the shapes of solids are converted into another shapes. In this process, the volume always remains the same. How does this happen? If you want a candle of any special shape, you have to heat the wax in metal container till it is completely melted. Then, you pour it into another container which has the special shape that you wanted. For example, lets us take a candle in the shape of solid cylinder, melt it and pour whole of the molten wax into another container shaped like a sphere. On cooling, you will obtain a candle in the shape of the sphere. 265 Mensuration XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 222777333 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::343307 PPPMMM The volume of the new candle will be the same as the volume of the earlier candle. In 1856, this peak was named after Sir George Everest, who had commissioned and first used the giant Theodolites. (i) The line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to a point on the object being viewed by the observer. (ii) The angle of elevation of the object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object. (i) The line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to a point on the object being viewed by the observer. (ii) The angle of elevation of the object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object. (iii) The angle of depression of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the object. 2. pages.text: Chapter 13 Probability A 13.1 Introduction N Kumar and Sudha were talking together while playing a carroms game: A Kumar: Do you think that you would win? G Sudha : There are 50 percent chances for that. I may win. Kumar: How do you say 50 percent? N Do you think Sudha is right in her statement? A Is her chance of wining 50%? Do you agree with her? L In this chapter, we study about such situations. We also discuss words like ‘probably’, E ‘likely’, ‘possibly’, etc. and how to quantify these. In class IX we studied about events that are extremely likely or almost certain andT those that are extremely unlikely and hence almost impossible. We also talked about chance, luck and the fact that an event occurs once does not mean that it would happen each time. In this chapter, we try to learn how the likelihood of an event can be , quantified. T This quantifiRcation into a numerical measure is referred to as finding 'Probability'. E 13.1.1 What is Probability C Consider an experiment: A normal coin was tossed 1000 times. Head turned up 455 times and tail turned up 545 times. If we try to find the likelihood of getting heads we may say it is 455 S 455 out of 1000 or or 0.455. 1000 This estimation of probability is based on the results of an actual experiment of tossing a coin 1000 times. These estimates are called experimental or empirical probabilities. In fact, all experimental probabilities are based on the results of actual experiments and an adequate recording of what happens in each of the events. These probabilities are only 'estimations'. If we perform the same experiment for another 1000 times, we may get slightly different data, giving different probability estimate. 309 Probability XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333111777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344420 PPPMMM

Many persons from different parts of the world have done this kind of experiment and recorded the number of heads that turned up. For example, the eighteenth century French naturalist Comte de Buffon, tossed a coin 4040 times and got 2048 times heads. The experimental probability of getting a head, in this 2048 A case, was  0.507. 4040 N J.E. Kerrich, from Britain, recorded 5067 heads in 10000 tosses of a coin. The experimental A 5067 probability of getting a head, in this case, was = 0.5067. English Statistician Karl Pearson 10000 G spent some more time, making 24000 tosses of a coin. He got 12012 times heads, and thus, the N experimental probability of a head obtained by him was 0.5005. A Now, suppose we ask, 'What will be the experimental probability of getting a head, if the experiment is carried on up to, say, 10 lakhs timLes? Or 1 crore times? You would intuitively feel that as the number of tosses increases, theE experimental probability of a head (or a tail) may settle 1 down closer and closer to the number 0.5 , i.e., . This matches the ‘theoretical probability’ of T2 getting a head (or getting a tail), about which we will learn now. This chapter is an introduction to the theoretical (also called c,lassical) probability of an event. T Now we discuss simple problems based on this concept. R 13.2 Probability - A Theoretical Approach E Let us consider the following situation: Suppose a ‘fair’ coin is tossed at random. C When we speak of a coin, we assume it to be 'fair', that is, it is symmetrical so that there is S no reason for it to come down more often on one side than the other. We call this property of the coin as being 'unbiased'. By the phrase 'random toss', we mean that the coin is allowed to fall freely without any bias or interference. These types of experiments are random experiments (Here we dismiss the possibility of its 'landing' on its edge, which may be possible, for example, if it falls on sand). We refer to this by saying that the outcomes, head and tail, are equally likely. Outcomes in an experiment are “equally likely” when chances of getting them are equal. For basic understanding of probability, in this chapter, we will assume that all the experiments have equally likely outcomes. 310 Probability XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333111888 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344420 PPPMMM

Do This a. Outcomes of which of the following experiments are equally likely? 1. Getting a digit 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 when a dice is rolled. 2. Selecting a different colour ball from a bag of 5 red balls, 4 blue balls and 1 black ball. 3. Winning in a game of carrom. A 4. Units place of a two digit number selected may be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. N 5. Selecting a different colour ball from a bag of 10 red balls, 10 blue balls and 10 black balls. A 6. Raining on a particular day of July. b. Are the outcomes of every experiment equally likely? G c. Give examples of 5 experiments that have equally likely outcomes and five more examples that do not have equally likely outcomes. N Activity A (i) Take any coin, toss it 50 times, 100 timLes and 150 times and count the number of times a head and a tail come up seperately. Record your observations in the following table:- E S. Number of Number of Probability of Number of Probability of T No. experiments heads head tails tails 1. 50 , T 2. 100 R 3. 150 What dEo you observe? Obviously, as the number of experiments increases, probability 1 of heCad or tail reaches 50% or . This empirical interpretation of probability can be applied 2 to every event associated with an experiment that can be repeated a large number of times. S Now, we know that the experimental or empirical probability P(E) of an event E is Number of trials in which the event happened P(E) = Total number of trials “The assumption of equally likely outcomes” (which is valid in many experiments, as in two of the examples seen, of a coin and of a dice) is one of the assumption that leads us to the following definition of probability of an event. Probability and Modelling The requirement of repeating an experiment has some limitations, as it may be very expensive or unfeasible in many situations. Of course, it worked well in the experiments of 311 Probability XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333111999 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344420 PPPMMM

tossing the coin or throwing a dice. But, how about repeating the experiment of launching a satellite in order to compute the empirical probability of its failure during launching, or the repetition of the phenomenon of an earthquake to compute the empirical probability of a multi-storeyed building getting destroyed in an earthquake? For finding these probabilities we calculate models of behaviour and use them to estimate behaviour and likely outcomes. Such models are complex and are validated by predictions and outcomes. Forecast of weather, A result of an election, population demography, earthquakes, crop production etc. are all based on such models and their predictions. N A The theoretical probability (also called classical probability) of an event T, written as P(T), is defined as G Number of outcomes favourable to T P(T) = N Number of all possible outcomes of the experiment where we assume that the outcomes of the expAeriment are equally likely. We usually simply refer to theoretical probability as Probability. L The definition of probability was given by Pierre Simon Laplace in 1795. E th Probability theory had its origin in the16 century when an Italian physician and T mathematician J. Cardan wrote the first book on the subject, The Book on Games of Chance. James B ernoulli (1654 -1705), A. De Moivre , (1667-1754), and PierreT Simon Laplace are among those who made significant contributions to this field. In recent years, probability has been R used extensively in many areas such as biology, economics, genetics, physics, socioElogy etc. 13.3C Mutually Exclusive Events Pierre Simon Laplace SIf a coin is tossed, we get a head or a tail, but not both. Similarly, (1749 – 1827) if we select a student of a high school that he/ she may belong to one of either 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10 classes, but not to any two or more classes. In both these examples, occurrence of an event prevents the occurrence of other events. Such events are called mutually exclusive events. Two or more events of an experiment, where occurence of an event prevents occurences of all other events, are called Mutually Exclusive Events. We will discuss this in more detail later in the chapter. 312 Probability XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333222000 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344420 PPPMMM

We consider the tossing of a coin as an event associated with experiments where the equally likely assumption holds. In order to proceed, we recall that there are two possible outcomes each time. This set of outcomes A is called the sample space. We can say that the “sample space” of one toss is {H, T}. For the experiment of drawing out a ball from a bag containing red, blue, yellow aNnd white ball, the sample space is {R, B, Y, W}. What is the sample space when a dice is thrown? A Do This G Think of 5 situations with equally likely events and find the sample space. N Let us now try to find the probability of equally likely events that are mutually exclusive. A Example-1. Find the probability of getting a head when a coin is tossed once. Also find the L probability of getting a tail. E Solution : In the experiment of tossing a coin once, the number of possible outcomes is two - Head (H) and Tail (T). Let E be the event 'getting a head'. The number of outcomes favourable T to E, (i.e., of getting a head) is 1. Therefore, Number of outcomes favourable to E 1 P(E) = P (head) = , = TNumber of all possible outcomes 2 Similarly, if F is the event 'getting a tail', then R 1 P(F) = P(tail) = (Guess why?) What is the probability that she takes a (i) yellow ball? (ii) red ball? (iii) blue ball? S Solution : Manasa takes out a ball from the bag without looking into it. So, it is equally likely that she takes out any one of them. Let Y be the event 'the ball taken out is yellow', B be the event 'the ball taken out is blue', and R be the event 'the ball taken out is red'. Now, the number of possible outcomes = 3. Similarly, in Example 2, all the three events, Y, B and R are elementary events. 2. In Example 1, we note that : P(E) + P(F) = 1 A In Example 2, we note that : P(Y) + P(R) + P(B) = 1. (ii) What is the probability of getting a number less than or equal to 4? Note : Are the events E and F in the above example elementary events? No, they are not elementary events. Then in example-3, weA calculated probability of events which are not elementary. We saw, 1 2 N P(E) + P(F) = + = 1 3 3 A Here, F is the same as 'not E' because there are only two events. We denote the event 'not E' by E. This is called the comGplement event of event E. So, P(E) + P(not E) = 1 N i.e., P(E) + P(E) = 1, which gives us P(E) = 1 - P(E). In general, it is true that for an event E,A P( ) = 1 – P(E) L Do This E (i) Is ‘getting a head’ complementary to ‘getting a tail’? Give reasons. R 13.3.3 Impossible and Certain Events Consider the following throws of a dice with sides marked as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. E (i) What is the probability of getting a number 7 in a single throw of a dice? C We know that there are only six possible outcomes in a single throw of this dice. These outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Since, no face of the dice is marked 7, there is no outcome S favourable to 7, i.e., the number of such outcomes is zero. In other words, getting 7 in a single throw of a dice, is impossible. Suppose E = outcome of getting 7. 0 So, P(E) = = 0 6 That is, the probability of an event which is impossible to occur is 0. Such an event is called an impossible event. (ii) What is the probability of getting 6 or a number less than 6 in a single throw of a dice? 315 Probability

Since, every face of a dice is marked with 6 or a number less than 6, it is sure that we will always get one of these when the dice is thrown once. So, the number of favourable outcomes is the same as the number of all possible outcomes, which is 6. Suppose E = (getting 6 or a number less than 6) 6 Therefore, P(E) = = 1 A 6 So, the probability of an event which is sure (or certain) to occur is 1. A deck of playing cards consists of 52 cards which are divided into 4 suits of 13 cards ª © ¨ § each. They are black spades ( ), red hearts ( ), red diamonds ( ) and black clubs ( ). 316 Probability

The cards in each suit are Ace, King, Queen, Jack, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2. Kings, Queens and Jacks are called face cards. Many games are played with this deck of cards. Some games are played with part of the deck and some with two decks even. The study of probability has a lot to do A with card and dice games as it helps players to estimate N possibilities and predict how A the cards could be distributed among players. G Example-4. One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Calculate the probability N that the card will (i) be an ace, (ii) not be an ace. A Solution : Well-shuffling ensures equally likely outcomes. (i) There are 4 aces in a deck. L Let E be the event 'the card is anE ace'. We know that in A sports some countries are strong and others are not so strong. We also know that when two players are playing it is not that they win equal times. The probability of Sange eta's winning chances = P(S) = 0.62 (given) , The probability Tof Reshma's winning chances = P(R) = 1 - P(S) = 1 -0.62 = 0.38 [R and S are complementary] R ExampleE-6. T 14.5 Which value of C entral Tendency? , T Which measure would be best suited for a particular requirement. The mean is the mRost frequently used measure of central tendency because it takes into account all the observations, and lies between the extremes, i.e., the largest and the smallest observations E of the entire data. It also enables us to compare two or more distributions. For example, by compaCring the average (mean) results of students of different schools of a particular examination, we can conclude which school has a better performance. S However, extreme values in the data affect the mean. For example, the mean of classes having frequencies more or less the same is a good representative of the data. But, if one class has frequency, say 2, and the five others have frequency 20, 25, 20, 21, 18, then the mean will certainly not reflect the way the data behaves. So, in such cases, the mean is not a good representative of the data. In problems where individual observations are not important, especially extreme values, and we wish to find out a ‘typical’ observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. These are situations where extreme values may exist. So, rather than the mean, we take the median as a better measure of central tendency. 349 Statistics XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333555777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

T 14.5 Which value of C entral Tendency? , T Which measure would be best suited for a particular requirement. The mean is the mRost frequently used measure of central tendency because it takes into account all the observations, and lies between the extremes, i.e., the largest and the smallest observations E of the entire data. It also enables us to compare two or more distributions. For example, by compaCring the average (mean) results of students of different schools of a particular examination, we can conclude which school has a better performance. S However, extreme values in the data affect the mean. For example, the mean of classes having frequencies more or less the same is a good representative of the data. But, if one class has frequency, say 2, and the five others have frequency 20, 25, 20, 21, 18, then the mean will certainly not reflect the way the data behaves. So, in such cases, the mean is not a good representative of the data. In problems where individual observations are not important, especially extreme values, and we wish to find out a ‘typical’ observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. These are situations where extreme values may exist. So, rather than the mean, we take the median as a better measure of central tendency. 349 Statistics XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333555777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM In situations which require establishing the most frequent value or most popular item, the mode is the best choice, e.g., to find the most popular T.V. programme being watched, the consumer item in greatest demand, the colour of the vehicle used by most of the people, etc. A Exercise - 14.3 N 1. T 14.5 Which value of C entral Tendency? , T Which measure would be best suited for a particular requirement. The mean is the mRost frequently used measure of central tendency because it takes into account all the observations, and lies between the extremes, i.e., the largest and the smallest observations E of the entire data. It also enables us to compare two or more distributions. For example, by compaCring the average (mean) results of students of different schools of a particular examination, we can conclude which school has a better performance. S However, extreme values in the data affect the mean. For example, the mean of classes having frequencies more or less the same is a good representative of the data. But, if one class has frequency, say 2, and the five others have frequency 20, 25, 20, 21, 18, then the mean will certainly not reflect the way the data behaves. So, in such cases, the mean is not a good representative of the data. In problems where individual observations are not important, especially extreme values, and we wish to find out a ‘typical’ observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. These are situations where extreme values may exist. So, rather than the mean, we take the median as a better measure of central tendency. 349 Statistics XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333555777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM In situations which require establishing the most frequent value or most popular item, the mode is the best choice, e.g., to find the most popular T.V. programme being watched, the consumer item in greatest demand, the colour of the vehicle used by most of the people, etc. A Exercise - 14.3 N 1. pages.text: Mathematical Modelling A A.I.1 Introduction N On 25th February 2013, the ISRO launcher PSLV C20, placed the satellite SARAL into orbit. The satellite weighs 407 kg. It is at an altitude of 781 km and its Aorbit is inclined at an angle of 98.5º. G On reading the above information, we may wonder: N (i) How did the scientists calculate the altitude as 781km. Did they go to space and measure it? A (ii) How did they conclude that the angle Lof orbit is 98.5º without actually measuring? E Some more examples are there in our daily life where we wonder how the scientists and mathematicians could possibly have estimated these results. Observe these examples: T (i) The temperature at the surface of the sun is about 6,000ºC. , (ii) The human heartT purifies 5 to 6 liters of blood in the body every minute. (iii) We know tRhat the distance between the sun and the earth is 149, 000,000 km. In the above examples, we know that no one went to the sun to measure the temperature E or the distance from earth. Nor can we take the heart out of the body and measure the blood it C pumps. How did they sine accurate answers to this type of questions. The way we answer these aSnd other similar questions is through mathematical modelling. Mathematical modelling is used not only by scientists but also by us. For example, we might want to know how much money we will get after one year if we invest D100 at 10% simple interest. Or we might want to know how many litres of paint is needed to whitewash a room. Even these problems are solved by mathematical modelling. Think and Discuss Discuss with your friends some more examples in real life where we cannot directly measure and must use mathematical modelling . Mathematical Modelling 357 XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666555 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

A.I.2 Mathematical Models Do you remember the formula to calculate the area of a triangle? 1 Area of Triangle =  base  height. 2 A PTR Similarly, simple interest calculation uses the formula I  . This formula or equation 100 N is a relation between the Interest (I); Principle (P); Time (T); and Rate of Interest (R). A These formulae are examples of mathematical models. G Some more examples for mathematical models. N Distance d (i) Speed (S)   time t A Lr n (ii) In compound interest sum (A) E = P   1 100     Where P =T Principle r = rate of interest , Tn = number of times interest is to be calculated. So, MathematicRal model is nothing but a mathematical description or relation that describes some real life situation. E C Do This S Write some more mathematical models which you have learnt in previous classes. A.I.3 Mathematical Modelling We often face problems in our day to day life. To solve them, we try to write it as an equivalent mathematical problem and find its solution. Next we interpret the solution and check to what extent the solution is valid. This process of constructing a mathematical model and using it to find the answer is known as mathematical modelling. 358 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666666 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

Now let us observe some more examples related to mathematical modelling. Example-1. Vani wants to buy a washing machine that costs `19,000 but she has only `15,000. So she decides to invest her money at 8% simple interest per year. After how many years will she be able to buy the washing machine ? Solution: A Step 1 : (Understanding the problem): In this stage, we define the real problem. Here, we are N given the principle, the rate of simple interest and we want to find out the number of years after A which the amount `15,000 will become Rs. 19000. Step 2 : (Mathematical description and formulation) In this sGtep, we describe, in mathematical terms, the different aspects of the problem. We define variables, write equations or inequalities N and gather data if required. A Here, we use the formula for simple interest which is L PTR I  (Model). Where 100 E P = Principle, T = numbeTr of years, R = rate of interest, I = Interest 100I We need to find time , T  TRP Step 3: (Solving tRhe mathematical problem) In this step, we solve the problem using the formula which we have developed in step 2. E We know that Vani already has `15,000 which is the principal, P C The final amount is `19000 so she needs an extra (19000-15000) = `4000. This will come from the interest, I . S 10040 0 0 400 P = `15,000, Rate = 8%, then I = 4000; T  1500 08 120 4 1 T3 3 years 12 3 or Step4 : (Interpreting the solution): The solution obtained in the previous step is interpreted here. 1 Here T = 3 . This means three and one third of a year or three years and 4 months. 3 So, Vani can buy a wahing mashine after 3 year 4 months Mathematical Modelling 359 XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

Step5 : (Validating the model): We can’t always accept a model that gives us an answer that does not match the reality. The process of checking and modifying the mathematical model, if necessary, is validation. In the given example, we are assuming that the rate of interest will not change. If the rate PTR changes then our model will not work. We are also assuming that the price of the washing 100 A machine will remain Rs. 19,000. N Let us take another example. A Example-2. In Lokeshwaram High school, 50 children in the 10th class and their Maths teacher G want to go on tour from Lokeshwaram to Hyderabad by vehicles. A jeep can hold six persons not including the driver. How many jeeps they need to hire? N Step 1 : We want to find the number of jeeps needed to carry 51 persons, given that each jeep can seat 6 persons besides the driver. A Step 2 : Number of vehicles = (Number of pLersons) / (Persons that can be seated in one jeep) Step 3 : Number of vehicles = 51/6 = E8.5 Step 4 : Interpretation T We know that it is not possible to have 8.5 vehicles. So, the number of vehicles needed has to be the nearest whole num ber which is 9. ,  Number of vTehicles need is 9. Step 5 : Validation R While modelling, we have assumed that lean and fat children occupy same space. E Otherwise this model will not useful to us. C Do This S 1. Select any verbal problem from your textbook, make a mathematical model for the selected problem and solve it. 2. Suppose a car starts from a place A and travels at a speed of 40 Km/h towards another place B. At the same time another car starts from B and travels towards A at a speed of 30 Km/h. If the distance between A and B is 100 km; after how much time will the cars meet? Make a mathematical model for the problem given above and solve it. 360 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666888 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

So far, we have made mathematical models for simple word problems. Let us take a real life example and model it. Example-3. In the year 2000, 191 member countries of the U.N.signed a declaration to promote gender equality. One indicator for deciding whether this goal has been achieved is the ratio of girls to boys in primary, secondary education. India also signed the declaration. The A data for the percentage of girls in India who are enrolled in primary schools is given in Table Table A.I.1 N Year Enrolment (in %) A 1991 – 92 41.9 G 1992 – 93 42.6 N 1993 – 94 42.7 A 1994 – 95 42.9 1995 – 96 4L3.1 E 1996 – 97 43.2 1997 -98 T43.5 1998 – 99 43.5 , 1999 T– 2000 43.6 R2000 – 01 43.7 E2001 - 02 44.1 Using this data, mathematically describe the rate at which the proportion of girls enrolled in C primary schools grew. Also, estimate the year by which the enrolment of girls will reach 50%. S Solution : Step 1 : Formulation Let us first convert the problem into a mathematical problem. Table A.I.1 gives the enrolment for the years 1991 – 92, 1992- 93 etc. Since the students join at the begining of an academic year, we can take the years as 1991, 1992 etc. Let us assume that the percentage of girls who join primary schools will continue to grow at the same rate as the rate in Table A.I.1. So, the number of years is important, not the specific years. (To give a similar situation, when we find the simple interest for say, ` 15000 at the rate 8% for three years, it does not matter whether the three – year period is from 1999 to 2002 or from 2001 to 2004. What is important is the interest rate in the years being considered) Mathematical Modelling 361 XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666999 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

At the end of the first year period from 1991 to 1992, the enrolment has increased by 0.7% from 41.9% to 42.6%. At the end of the second year, this has increased by 0.1% from 42.6% to 42.7%. From the table above, we cannot find a definite relationship between the number of years and percentage. But the increase is fairly steady. So, the Enrolment Percentage (EP) iLn the first year = 41.9 + 0.22 E EP in the second year = 41.9 + 0.22 + 0.22 = 41.9 + 2  0.22 T EP in the third year = 41.9 + 0.22 + 0.22 + 0.22 = 41.9 + 3  0.22 So, the enrolment percentage in the nth year = 41.9 + 0.22n, for n 1. .... Let us find the values for the years we already know, using Formula (2), and compare it with the known values by finding the difference. The values are given in Table A.I.4. A.I.4 Advantages of Mathematics Modelling 1. The aim of mathematical modelling is to get some useful information about a real world problem by converting it into mathematical problem. This is especially useful when it is not possible or very expensive to get information by other means such as direct observation or by conducting experiments. A For example, suppose we want to study the corrosive effect of the discharge of the Mathura refinery on the Taj Mahal. We would not like to carry ouNt experiments on the Taj Mahal directly because that would damage a valuable monument. Here mathematical A modelling can be of great use. 2. Forecasting is very important in many types of organizGations, since predictions of future events have to be incorporated into the decision – making process. N For example (i) In marketing departments, reliable forecasts of demand help in planning of the A sale strategies L (ii) A school board needs to able to forecast the increase in the number of school going children in variouEs districts so as to decide where and when to start new schools. T 3. Often we need to estimate large values like trees in a forest; fishes in a lake; estimation of votes polled etc. , Some more examTples where we use mathematical modelling are: (i) Estimating future population for certain number of years R (ii) Predicting the arrival of Monsoon E (iii) Estimating the literacy rate in coming years C(iv) Estimating number of leaves in a tree (v) Finding the depth of oceans S A.I.5 Limitations of Mathematical modelling Is mathematical modelling the answer to all our problems? Certainly not; it has it’s limitations. Thus, we should keep in mind that a model is only a simplification of a real world problem, and the two are not same. It is some thing like the difference between a map that gives the physical features of a country, and the country itself. We can find the height of a place above the sea level from this map, but we cannot find the characteristics of the people from it. So, we should use a model only for the purpose it is supposed to serve, remembering all the factors we have neglected while constructing it. We should apply the model only within the limits where it is applicable. 366 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333777444 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344643 PPPMMM

A.I.6 To What Extent We Should Try To Improve Our Model? To improve a model we need to take into account several additional factors. When we do this we add more variables to our mathematical equations. The equations becomes complicated and the model is difficult to use. A model must be simple enough to use yet accurate; i.e the closer it is to reality the better the model is. A Try This N A problem dating back to the early 13th century, posed by Leonardo Fibonacci, asks A how many rabbits you would have in one year if you started with just two and let all of them reproduce. Assume that a pair of rabbits produces a pair of offspring each month and that G each pair of rabbits produces their first offspring at the age of 2 months. Month by month, the number of pairs of rabbits is given by the sum of the Nrabbits in the two preceding months, except for the 0th and the 1st months. A Step 2 (Mathematical description) : In mathematical terms, the problem translates to finding out the probabilities of the various possible sums of numbers tGhat the dice could show. N Before going to the next try this exercise, we need some background information. A Not having the money you want when you need it, is a common experience for many people. Whether it is having enough money for buying essentials for daily living, or for buying G comforts, we always require money. To enable the customers with limited funds to purchase goods like scooters, refrigerators, televisions, cars, etc., aN scheme known as an instalment scheme (or plan) is introduced by traders. A Sometimes a trader introduces an instalment scheme as a marketing strategy to allow L customers to purchase these articles. Under the instalment scheme, the customer is not required to make full payment of the article at theE time of buying it. She/he is allowed to pay a part of it at the time of purchase and the rest can be paid in instalments, which could be monthly, quarterly, T half-yearly, or even yearly. Of course, the buyer will have to pay more in the instalment plan, because the seller is going to charge some interest on account of the payment made at a later date , (called deferred paymenTt). There are sRome frequently used terms related to this concept. You may be familiar with them. For example, the cost price of an article is the amount which a customer has to pay as full E payment of the article at the time it is purchased. Cash down payment is the amount which a customCer has to pay as part payment of the price of an article at the time of purchase. Now, try to solve the problem given below by using mathematical modelling. S Try This Ravi wants to buy a bicycle. He goes to the market and finds that the bicycle of his choice costs `2,400. He has only `1,400 with him. To help, the shopkeepr offers to help him. He says that Ravi can make a down payment of `1400 and pay the rest in monthly instalments of `550 each. Ravi can either take the shopkeepers offer or go to a bank and take a loan at 12% per annum simple interest. From these two opportunities which is the best one to Ravi. Help him. chapters.fullText: Mathematical Modelling A A.I.1 Introduction N On 25th February 2013, the ISRO launcher PSLV C20, placed the satellite SARAL into orbit. The satellite weighs 407 kg. It is at an altitude of 781 km and its Aorbit is inclined at an angle of 98.5º. G On reading the above information, we may wonder: N (i) How did the scientists calculate the altitude as 781km. Did they go to space and measure it? A (ii) How did they conclude that the angle Lof orbit is 98.5º without actually measuring? E Some more examples are there in our daily life where we wonder how the scientists and mathematicians could possibly have estimated these results. Observe these examples: T (i) The temperature at the surface of the sun is about 6,000ºC. , (ii) The human heartT purifies 5 to 6 liters of blood in the body every minute. (iii) We know tRhat the distance between the sun and the earth is 149, 000,000 km. In the above examples, we know that no one went to the sun to measure the temperature E or the distance from earth. Nor can we take the heart out of the body and measure the blood it C pumps. How did they sine accurate answers to this type of questions. The way we answer these aSnd other similar questions is through mathematical modelling. Mathematical modelling is used not only by scientists but also by us. For example, we might want to know how much money we will get after one year if we invest D100 at 10% simple interest. Or we might want to know how many litres of paint is needed to whitewash a room. Even these problems are solved by mathematical modelling. The aim of mathematical modelling is to get some useful information about a real world problem by converting it into mathematical problem. This is especially useful when it is not possible or very expensive to get information by other means such as direct observation or by conducting experiments. A For example, suppose we want to study the corrosive effect of the discharge of the Mathura refinery on the Taj Mahal. We would not like to carry ouNt experiments on the Taj Mahal directly because that would damage a valuable monument. Here mathematical A modelling can be of great use. 2. Forecasting is very important in many types of organizGations, since predictions of future events have to be incorporated into the decision – making process. N For example (i) In marketing departments, reliable forecasts of demand help in planning of the A sale strategies L (ii) A school board needs to able to forecast the increase in the number of school going children in variouEs districts so as to decide where and when to start new schools. T 3. Often we need to estimate large values like trees in a forest; fishes in a lake; estimation of votes polled etc. , Some more examTples where we use mathematical modelling are: (i) Estimating future population for certain number of years R (ii) Predicting the arrival of Monsoon E (iii) Estimating the literacy rate in coming years C(iv) Estimating number of leaves in a tree (v) Finding the depth of oceans S A.I.5 Limitations of Mathematical modelling Is mathematical modelling the answer to all our problems? Certainly not; it has it’s limitations. Thus, we should keep in mind that a model is only a simplification of a real world problem, and the two are not same. It is some thing like the difference between a map that gives the physical features of a country, and the country itself. We can find the height of a place above the sea level from this map, but we cannot find the characteristics of the people from it. So, we should use a model only for the purpose it is supposed to serve, remembering all the factors we have neglected while constructing it. We should apply the model only within the limits where it is applicable. 366 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333777444 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344643 PPPMMM A.I.6 To What Extent We Should Try To Improve Our Model? Observe these examples: T (i) The temperature at the surface of the sun is about 6,000ºC. , (ii) The human heartT purifies 5 to 6 liters of blood in the body every minute.
