This formula or equation 100 N is a relation between the Interest (I); Principle (P); Time (T); and Rate of Interest (R). A These formulae are examples of mathematical models. So, MathematicRal model is nothing but a mathematical description or relation that describes some real life situation. E C Do This S Write some more mathematical models which you have learnt in previous classes. A.I.3 Mathematical Modelling We often face problems in our day to day life. To solve them, we try to write it as an equivalent mathematical problem and find its solution. Next we interpret the solution and check to what extent the solution is valid. This process of constructing a mathematical model and using it to find the answer is known as mathematical modelling. 358 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666666 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM Now let us observe some more examples related to mathematical modelling. Example-1. Vani wants to buy a washing machine that costs `19,000 but she has only `15,000. So she decides to invest her money at 8% simple interest per year. After how many years will she be able to buy the washing machine ? Solution: A Step 1 : (Understanding the problem): In this stage, we define the real problem. Here, we are N given the principle, the rate of simple interest and we want to find out the number of years after A which the amount `15,000 will become Rs. 19000. Step 2 : (Mathematical description and formulation) In this sGtep, we describe, in mathematical terms, the different aspects of the problem. We define variables, write equations or inequalities N and gather data if required. A Here, we use the formula for simple interest which is L PTR I  (Model). Where 100 E P = Principle, T = numbeTr of years, R = rate of interest, I = Interest 100I We need to find time , T  TRP Step 3: (Solving tRhe mathematical problem) In this step, we solve the problem using the formula which we have developed in step 2. E We know that Vani already has `15,000 which is the principal, P C The final amount is `19000 so she needs an extra (19000-15000) = `4000. This will come from the interest, I . S 10040 0 0 400 P = `15,000, Rate = 8%, then I = 4000; T  1500 08 120 4 1 T3 3 years 12 3 or Step4 : (Interpreting the solution): The solution obtained in the previous step is interpreted here. 1 Here T = 3 . This means three and one third of a year or three years and 4 months. 3 So, Vani can buy a wahing mashine after 3 year 4 months Mathematical Modelling 359 XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666777 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM Step5 : (Validating the model): We can’t always accept a model that gives us an answer that does not match the reality. The process of checking and modifying the mathematical model, if necessary, is validation. In the given example, we are assuming that the rate of interest will not change. If the rate PTR changes then our model will not work. We are also assuming that the price of the washing 100 A machine will remain Rs. 19,000. N Let us take another example. A Example-2. In Lokeshwaram High school, 50 children in the 10th class and their Maths teacher G want to go on tour from Lokeshwaram to Hyderabad by vehicles. A jeep can hold six persons not including the driver. How many jeeps they need to hire? N Step 1 : We want to find the number of jeeps needed to carry 51 persons, given that each jeep can seat 6 persons besides the driver. A Step 2 : Number of vehicles = (Number of pLersons) / (Persons that can be seated in one jeep) Step 3 : Number of vehicles = 51/6 = E8.5 Step 4 : Interpretation T We know that it is not possible to have 8.5 vehicles. So, the number of vehicles needed has to be the nearest whole num ber which is 9. ,  Number of vTehicles need is 9. Step 5 : Validation R While modelling, we have assumed that lean and fat children occupy same space. E Otherwise this model will not useful to us. C Do This S 1. Select any verbal problem from your textbook, make a mathematical model for the selected problem and solve it. 2. Suppose a car starts from a place A and travels at a speed of 40 Km/h towards another place B. At the same time another car starts from B and travels towards A at a speed of 30 Km/h. If the distance between A and B is 100 km; after how much time will the cars meet? Make a mathematical model for the problem given above and solve it. 360 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666888 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM So far, we have made mathematical models for simple word problems. Let us take a real life example and model it. Example-3. In the year 2000, 191 member countries of the U.N.signed a declaration to promote gender equality. One indicator for deciding whether this goal has been achieved is the ratio of girls to boys in primary, secondary education. India also signed the declaration. The A data for the percentage of girls in India who are enrolled in primary schools is given in Table Table A.I.1 N Year Enrolment (in %) A 1991 – 92 41.9 G 1992 – 93 42.6 N 1993 – 94 42.7 A 1994 – 95 42.9 1995 – 96 4L3.1 E 1996 – 97 43.2 1997 -98 T43.5 1998 – 99 43.5 , 1999 T– 2000 43.6 R2000 – 01 43.7 E2001 - 02 44.1 Using this data, mathematically describe the rate at which the proportion of girls enrolled in C primary schools grew. Also, estimate the year by which the enrolment of girls will reach 50%. S Solution : Step 1 : Formulation Let us first convert the problem into a mathematical problem. Table A.I.1 gives the enrolment for the years 1991 – 92, 1992- 93 etc. Since the students join at the begining of an academic year, we can take the years as 1991, 1992 etc. Let us assume that the percentage of girls who join primary schools will continue to grow at the same rate as the rate in Table A.I.1. So, the number of years is important, not the specific years. (To give a similar situation, when we find the simple interest for say, ` 15000 at the rate 8% for three years, it does not matter whether the three – year period is from 1999 to 2002 or from 2001 to 2004. What is important is the interest rate in the years being considered) Mathematical Modelling 361 XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333666999 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344642 PPPMMM

The aim of mathematical modelling is to get some useful information about a real world problem by converting it into mathematical problem. This is especially useful when it is not possible or very expensive to get information by other means such as direct observation or by conducting experiments. A For example, suppose we want to study the corrosive effect of the discharge of the Mathura refinery on the Taj Mahal. We would not like to carry ouNt experiments on the Taj Mahal directly because that would damage a valuable monument. Here mathematical A modelling can be of great use. 2. Forecasting is very important in many types of organizGations, since predictions of future events have to be incorporated into the decision – making process. N For example (i) In marketing departments, reliable forecasts of demand help in planning of the A sale strategies L (ii) A school board needs to able to forecast the increase in the number of school going children in variouEs districts so as to decide where and when to start new schools. T 3. Often we need to estimate large values like trees in a forest; fishes in a lake; estimation of votes polled etc. , Some more examTples where we use mathematical modelling are: (i) Estimating future population for certain number of years R (ii) Predicting the arrival of Monsoon E (iii) Estimating the literacy rate in coming years C(iv) Estimating number of leaves in a tree (v) Finding the depth of oceans S A.I.5 Limitations of Mathematical modelling Is mathematical modelling the answer to all our problems? Certainly not; it has it’s limitations. Thus, we should keep in mind that a model is only a simplification of a real world problem, and the two are not same. It is some thing like the difference between a map that gives the physical features of a country, and the country itself. We can find the height of a place above the sea level from this map, but we cannot find the characteristics of the people from it. So, we should use a model only for the purpose it is supposed to serve, remembering all the factors we have neglected while constructing it. We should apply the model only within the limits where it is applicable. 366 Mathematical Modelling XXX MMMaaattthhheeemmmaaatttiiicccsss EEEMMM FFFiiinnnaaalll 222555---111000---222000222444...pppdddfff 333777444 111000///222555///222000222444 111:::222123:::344643 PPPMMM

keyPoints: One indicator for deciding whether this goal has been achieved is the ratio of girls to boys in primary, secondary education.
Also, estimate the year by which the enrolment of girls will reach 50%.
S Solution : Step 1 : Formulation Let us first convert the problem into a mathematical problem.
Table A.I.1 gives the enrolment for the years 1991 – 92, 1992- 93 etc.
Since the students join at the begining of an academic year, we can take the years as 1991, 1992 etc.
Let us assume that the percentage of girls who join primary schools will continue to grow at the same rate as the rate in Table A.I.1.
So, the number of years is important, not the specific years.

(To give a similar situation, when we find the simple interest for say, ` 15000 at the rate 8% for three years, it does not matter whether the three – year period is from 1999 to 2002 or from 2001 to 2004.
Here also, we will see how the enrolment grows after 1991 by comparing the number of years that has passed after 1991 and the enrolment.
Let us take 1991 as the 0 th year, and write 1 for 1992 since 1 year has passed in 1992 after 1991.
